style.vernacular: A dense hillside city-state on the Riviera: Belle Epoque and Beaux-Arts buildings in cream limestone and warm ochre, apricot, pink and pale yellow render with stucco ornament, wrought-iron balconies and green shutters; the Rock of Monaco-Ville has medieval Genoese-Italian houses in pastel render and a Louis XIV-style palace; modern Fontvieille is reclaimed land with white and cream mid-rise blocks with terraces and balconies; high-rises and glass towers climb the slopes. Mansard roofs in zinc or slate, terracotta tile, copper cupolas with green patina; palms, pines, agave and bougainvillea.
style.ornament: Garnier-era Beaux-Arts: carved pediments, caryatids, balustrades, twin ornate towers, wrought-iron balconies, striped awnings; Genoese pastel render with shutters and trompe-l oeil window frames on the Rock; Baroque Revival cliff-front staircases; terraces and balconies throughout.

sources.what: French Belle Epoque with Italian/Genoese influence, Louis XIV palace, cream-coloured stone cathedral, locally sourced granite, marble and terracotta tile in modern buildings, coloured turrets, terraces and balconies. Specific hex colours are from general photographic knowledge of Monaco rather than a citation.
Fontvieille is reclaimed land, built from 1966; parks, stadium, heliport and museums there

style.vernacular: Low city of timber houses clad in corrugated iron painted red, blue, yellow, green and white with contrasting roofs and window frames; cheap reinforced-concrete houses and apartment blocks from the early 20th century on, often painted or finished with a dashed mineral/shell render in white, cream or grey; functionalist and modernist concrete public buildings with flat or low roofs; steel-and-glass towers and halls (Harpa) and big-box malls on the edges. Few trees (birch, spruce), lava fields and treeless coast around.
style.ornament: Corrugated iron cladding in bright paint, white window frames, steep gabled roofs on old houses and low flat roofs on modernist ones, gable-fronted concrete houses of the Guðjón Samúelsson school, basalt-column motifs in civic buildings, lava rock and moss as landscaping.

sources.what: corrugated iron cladding as a distinctly Icelandic feature, bright painted wooden houses, early concrete houses, steep pitched and low modernist roofs, functionalism from the 1930s with mineral and seashell dashed finishes, turf houses

style.vernacular: Small, humid equatorial island capital with a Portuguese colonial core: low pastel plastered buildings (pink, cream, yellow, pale green) with white trim, timber balconies and verandahs and rusty corrugated or clay-tile roofs; outside the centre are cement-block houses and wooden stilt houses, and former cocoa-plantation roças with a long white main house, a hospital and rows of workers' houses around a drying terrace. Greenery is lush: palms, breadfruit, cocoa and forest right up to the town.
style.ornament: Portuguese neoclassical columns, window surrounds and entrance staircases on official buildings; timber verandahs with balustrades and fretwork on roça houses; tall iron fences; white-painted trim against pastel walls.

style.vernacular: Valley city of layered eras: Ottoman Baščaršija with low whitewashed and stone shops, timber-framed upper storeys and domed stone halls; Austro-Hungarian centre of ochre, cream and pink rendered blocks in Secession and Moorish Revival dress; socialist-era concrete and render housing blocks in Novi Grad and Dobrinja; hillside houses stepping up the slopes under red-orange clay-tile hip roofs; new glass towers (Sead Gološ designs) in Marijin Dvor.
style.ornament: Ottoman: overhanging timber upper storeys, wooden eaves, stone domes and lead roofs, pseudo-Ottoman Sebilj fountain, minarets; Austro-Hungarian: Secession and Moorish Revival friezes, banded stone, cornices; socialist era: bare concrete and render blocks, bullet-scarred walls with red-resin Sarajevo Roses.

sources.what: city architecture: Ottoman Baščaršija core, Austro-Hungarian centre (Secession, Moorish Revival), socialist blocks in Novi Grad, hillside houses

style.vernacular: Nordic capital: ochre, yellow and cream plastered apartment blocks of four to six storeys from the 19th and early 20th century with copper-green or dark sheet roofs; red-brick National Romantic buildings; pale functionalist blocks of the 1930s; Million Programme concrete and render housing suburbs; Falu red timber cottages in the archipelago; medieval fieldstone churches in the countryside; glass-and-metal malls and offices in the suburbs.

style.vernacular: Vilnius mixes a pastel Baroque and neoclassical Old Town (plastered brick in ochre, salmon, cream and pale green with white trim, red tile or grey metal roofs), red-brick Gothic and Renaissance churches, timber villas in Zverynas and the villages, and a Soviet belt of grey and pale panel apartment blocks, brick institutes and concrete civic buildings, with new glass offices around the Neris. Steep roofs shed snow; pine, birch and spruce surround most buildings.

style.vernacular: Swiss lake-and-river city: medieval Altstadt of narrow 3-4 storey eaves-to-street houses in plaster/whitewash and sandstone with steep clay-tile roofs; late 19th-century Gruenderzeit stone-faced blocks with mansard or hip roofs; interwar Neues Bauen and 1950s-70s concrete modernism; glass-and-steel offices in Oerlikon/Zuerich-West; surrounding villages and towns (Winterthur, Baden, Bremgarten, lake-side Pfannenstiel) of render houses with timber shutters, gabled/hipped tile roofs and baroque church towers with onion or spire helms.
